Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

name: arc-grid-reasoning
description: Use for ARC puzzle solving.
---

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use for ARC-like grid puzzles involving noisy backgrounds, repeated shapes, recoloring, symmetry, and demonstrations.

## Workflow
1. Record exact dimensions, colors, and changed cells from each demo. Use coordinates or a script instead of visual impressions alone.
2. Identify background and foreground objects; group connected components and infer each object's role from demos.
3. Extract shapes as exact occupied coordinate sets relative to bounding-box origin, preserving holes and irregular edges.
4. Test candidate rules against demos. Require exact changed-cell agreement; consider rotations/reflections only if supported.
5. Re-extract the exemplar from every fresh test input. A demo establishes the rule, not necessarily a reusable stencil.
6. Apply only required changes. Verify dimensions, cell range, row lengths, and preservation of untouched cells. Revisit shape, object role, symmetry, and overlap after incorrect feedback.

## Repeated-shape recoloring
When a distinctive colored object acts as a stencil and matching background patterns are recolored to its color, locate exact occupied-cell matches. Keep the exemplar and unrelated cells unchanged. See `references/stencil-matching.md` for a procedure and demo-derived example.

## Pitfalls
- Do not reuse a demo stencil without checking the fresh test's exemplar.
- Do not include neighboring noise or omit cells from the stencil.
- Do not fill an object's bounding rectangle; match its exact mask.
- Investigate overlapping candidate matches instead of silently dropping them.
- Do not assume rotations or reflections are allowed without evidence.
- Prefer mechanical validation over hand-transcribing a full grid.

{"success": true, "name": "arc-grid-reasoning", "file": "references/diagonal-periodic-lattice-decoding.md", "content": "# Decoding diagonal periodic lattices into tiled grids

A common ARC construction encodes a periodic color sequence using parallel diagonal lines (often colored sample cells lie on one or more diagonals). The output may be a fully filled periodic grid, not a modification of the sparse input.

## Reliable procedure
1. From each demo output, identify the smallest repeating 2D tile and verify it across rows and columns. Do not infer the tile only from one visible input diagonal.
2. Compare the input's distinctive colored coordinates against output values at the corresponding coordinates. Test candidate invariants such as `(r+c) mod p`, `(c-r) mod p`, and direct row/column periods. Use zero- or one-based coordinates consistently; shift can change phase.
3. Build a ledger from every nonzero input marker `(r,c,color)` to the output value at the same cell. Check for collisions: markers mapping to the same residue must agree. Use multiple demo pairs and varying dimensions to establish the period and phase.
4. Ensure the proposed mapping predicts every output cell in every demo, not merely the colored anchors. A sequence observed along a diagonal may be traversed in the opposite direction when propagated to rows.
5. Apply the validated rule to the fresh test and mechanically validate exact dimensions, all row lengths, legal colors, and the full coordinate formula.

## Important caution
Sparse lattice markers can have several plausible modular explanations when only a few colors or residues are sampled. A small period that seems visually obvious can be wrong. If competing periods/orientations predict different test grids, request a targeted demo; otherwise derive the mapping jointly from all examples. Do not spend multiple demo turns without analyzing each returned pair, and do not submit a generated grid unless the final action is actually the intended `submit` JSON.

This technique overlaps with `references/periodic-grid-compression.md` and the interactive stream skill's demo/action discipline; use this reference for diagonal periodic fill specifically.", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-ws0/frozen/seen/play/users/u012/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/arc-grid-reasoning/references/diagonal-periodic-lattice-decoding.md"}

When the input is a large periodic lattice but the target output is a small matrix, do not infer that output from dimensions or intuitive reading. Treat demonstrations as exact encoding examples.

## Analysis procedure
1. Record input and output dimensions for each pair. Note candidate row/column periods and the full set of exceptional values at lattice intersections or separators.
2. Find the periodic cell structure. Separate the repeated background/lines from marker positions; identify which rows/columns contain anchors or signal changes.
3. Build candidate decoders that map exact input coordinates, local cells, or repeated blocks to output cells. Include a candidate only if it explains every output value and placement in all demos.
4. Explicitly test special cases: absent markers, repeated colors, asymmetric markers, border elements, and examples with different period/dimensions. Distinguish orientation and reading-order hypotheses.
5. If viable rules produce different test outputs, request another demo with a named distinguishing prediction. Do not submit speculative output shapes.
6. Decode the fresh test using the validated rule. Verify output height/width, row lengths, and every decoded cell against its source evidence.

## Failure prevention
- A tiny output is not necessarily the input's marker row or the first few special cells.
- Multiple apparent marker rows/columns may represent different output rows/columns; don't collapse them without evidence.
- Preserve row-major/column-major or other ordering only when demos establish it.
- After a wrong submission, identify which decoding assumption failed; never cycle through arbitrary output dimensions or value variants.
- In a strict one-action stream, use the permitted demo budget to resolve actual ambiguity rather than spending multiple wrong submissions on ungrounded guesses.

This procedure complements the general exact-delta and retry guidance in the parent ARC skill.", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-ws0/frozen/seen/play/users/u012/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/arc-grid-reasoning/references/periodic-grid-compression.md"}
